title: Faith, and Knowledge with It
sum: The letter opens without names. The writer greets "sons and daughters" whom he once spoke among (1:4), rejoices that the Spirit has been poured out on them, and says he loves them more than his own life. He writes so that "along with your faith you may have perfect knowledge" (1:5).

He sets out three teachings of the Lord (hope, righteousness and love, in the form Lake prints, 1:6), says the Master has shown through the prophets what is past and present and given a taste of what is to come (1:7), and promises to point out a few things "not as a teacher, but as one of you" (1:8). The "knowledge" he means is the hidden meaning of Scripture, which fills chapters 2-17.

views.H: No author, place or date is named. Lake calls the letter "really anonymous" and the tradition that Paul's companion Barnabas wrote it "generally regarded as impossible to accept." The jumbled list in 1:6, where each witness differs, shows how unsettled the text was.
views.N: The poured-out Spirit (1:3) is the language of Acts 2 and Titus 3:6; faith, hope and love (1:4-6) recall 1 Corinthians 13:13 and 1 Thessalonians 1:3.
views.T: "Knowledge" (gnōsis) is the key word of the method: faith receives the Scriptures, knowledge reads their figures. The writer promises a reading of past, present and future, the three times of 1:7.
views.C: Clement of Alexandria quoted the letter as Scripture, Lake says. Ladeuze finds that the writer, though he touches points the Gnostics later argued, "has no knowledge of these latter": his knowledge is about reading Scripture, not secret myths.

echoes: Acts 2:17-18; Titus 3:6; 1 Corinthians 13:13; 1 Thessalonians 1:3; 1 Corinthians 8:1

settings.what: The greeting and purpose of the letter
settings.by: The writer, who never gives his name
settings.to: Christian "sons and daughters" among whom he had once spoken (1:4)
settings.when: after a visit to them, now apart from them
settings.why: To renew his bond with them and to say why he writes: to add "perfect knowledge" to their faith, so they read the Scriptures rightly in evil days.
settings.readers: Christians the writer had taught and loves (1:4-5). Ladeuze (Catholic Encyclopedia) reads 1:2-4 and 21:7-9 as a letter to "a particular church" in which the writer had been a teacher and from which he was now away. Who they were is argued: Ladeuze finds it "impossible to believe that either he or the larger part of his readers were of Jewish origin"; the Jewish Encyclopedia, after Güdemann, takes the writer for "a converted Jew." Lake places them in a community "in which Alexandrian ideas prevailed" and dates the letter to "the end of the first or beginning of the second century"; Ladeuze dates it to AD 130-131.

title: Not Sacrifices but a Crushed Heart
sum: The days are evil and the devil has power, so believers must search out the Lord's decrees, helped by fear, endurance, patience and self-control (2:1-3).

The prophets show that God needs no sacrifices. Barnabas quotes Isaiah 1:11-13 and joins Jeremiah 7:22-23 to Zechariah 8:17. God "did away with these things," so that "the new law of our Lord Jesus Christ" would have an offering not made by human hands: a crushed heart that gives glory to its maker (2:6-10). The words to Israel are "to them"; the words about the true sacrifice are "to us."
readings: Read as the prophets meant it
Isaiah and Jeremiah attack sacrifice offered by people who do wrong. Read this way, Barnabas's quotations support a call to justice and a humble heart, which every reader can accept.
The rites were never God's will; Israel misread its own prophets. Read this way, the chapter is the first step in the letter's case against keeping the law.

views.H: The quotations follow the Septuagint and are sometimes joined from two prophets (2:7-8), a habit of early Christian proof texts. The second half of 2:10 is in no known book.
views.J: In the prophets the critique of sacrifice stands beside promises of right offerings (Isaiah 56:7; Malachi 3:3-4), so it reads as a call to justice with worship, not as a rejection of worship.
views.N: Hebrews 10:1-10 quotes Psalm 40 to say Christ's offering of himself replaced the sacrifices. Barnabas says they were never wanted; Hebrews says they were a shadow now fulfilled.
views.T: The method begins here: the plain sense (sacrifice) is said to the people, the real sense (the heart) to us.
views.C: The "new law of our Lord Jesus Christ" (2:6) is the letter's own phrase; compare "the law of Christ" (Galatians 6:2).

echoes: Isaiah 1:11-14; Jeremiah 7:22-23; Zechariah 8:17; Psalm 51:16-17; Hosea 6:6; Hebrews 10:1-10; Matthew 11:29-30

settings.what: The writer's argument from the prophets
settings.by: The writer, quoting Isaiah 1, Jeremiah 7, Zechariah 8 and Psalm 51
settings.when: in "evil days" (2:1)
settings.why: To show that God never wanted the sacrifices, so that the readers will not think they must keep the law's rites. In the prophets the words were said to Israel to call it back to justice; Barnabas divides them into words "to them" and "to us."

settings.by: The Lord, through Isaiah
settings.to: in Isaiah, Judah and Jerusalem; in Barnabas, "them," the Jews
settings.when: Isaiah: the 700s BC, under kings of Judah
settings.why: In Isaiah, to shame worshipers whose hands are full of blood (Isaiah 1:15-17). In Barnabas, to prove that God never wanted sacrifice at all.

title: The Fast God Chose
sum: Barnabas quotes Isaiah 58:4-10 in the Greek and splits it in two. To "them" God says that bowing the head and lying in sackcloth is not the fast he chose (3:1-2). To "us" he says the fast he chose is to loosen the bonds of wrongdoing, set the crushed free, feed the hungry and clothe the naked; then light will break out and God will answer, "Look, I am here" (3:3-5).

The patient God showed all this beforehand, so that "we would not be shipwrecked by joining their law like newcomers" (3:6). The danger is now named: Christians who would take up the Jewish law as converts do.

views.H: The variant in 3:4 ("clothes" in the manuscripts, "healing" in the Greek Isaiah) is a good example of Lake's rule: print what the copies say, even when a correction is probably what the writer meant.
views.J: Isaiah 58 calls Israel's own fasting to become justice. Barnabas uses the same chapter to separate the church from the synagogue's fast.
views.N: Jesus teaches that fasting must not be for show (Matthew 6:16-18), and his own sermon at Nazareth uses Isaiah 58:6 inside Isaiah 61 (Luke 4:18, "to send the crushed away free").
views.T: The division of one prophecy into words to "them" and to "us" is the letter's basic tool.

echoes: Isaiah 58:4-10; Matthew 6:16-18; Luke 4:18; James 1:27; Galatians 5:1-4

settings.by: The Lord, through Isaiah, as the writer arranges the passage
settings.to: in Isaiah, Israel; in Barnabas, "them" (3:1-2) and "us" (3:3-5)
settings.when: Isaiah: after the return from exile, when fasting had become a ritual
settings.why: In Isaiah, to turn Israel's fasting into justice for the poor. In Barnabas, to show his readers that the true fast is justice, so that they will not take up the Jewish law (3:6).
settings.readers: Readers the writer fears might be "shipwrecked" by taking on "their law" like converts (3:6). Ladeuze finds nothing in the letter to show they were really in that danger.

title: The Stumbling Block Draws Near
sum: The end is near. Barnabas urges his readers to run from lawlessness and from the error of the present time (4:1-2). The "complete stumbling block" of which "Enoch" speaks has come near, and Daniel's ten kingdoms and the small king who brings down three are at work (4:3-5).

Then comes the letter's sharpest claim. Some say "the covenant is theirs and ours"; Barnabas says it is ours alone, because Israel lost it when Moses broke the tablets (4:6-8). The readers must stand firm in the last days, gather together rather than keep apart (4:10), remember that the Lord judges without favoritism (4:12), and not doze off, "as it is written," lest they be found "many called, but few chosen" (4:14).

views.H: Two dating arguments start here. Lake reports that the ten kings of 4:4-5 have been counted as Roman emperors, giving a first-century date, "though there is no unanimity" on how to count them, and judges that neither this nor the Temple argument of 16:3-4 "is quite satisfactory."
views.J: Barnabas claims Israel lost the covenant at Sinai. Exodus 34 says God renewed it, and Jeremiah 31:35-37 says Israel will not cease to be a nation before God. The claim is the heart of what the Jewish Encyclopedia calls the letter's "anti-Judaic spirit of great bitterness."
views.N: "As it is written" before Matthew 22:14 treats a Gospel saying as Scripture. Paul's Romans 9:4 and 11:1-2, 28-29 say the opposite of 4:6-8 about Israel and the covenants.
views.T: The broken tablets become a figure: the stone covenant shattered so that the covenant of Jesus could be sealed in the heart (4:8), as in Jeremiah 31:33 and 2 Corinthians 3:3.
views.C: Codex Sinaiticus placed this letter right after Revelation, Lake says, so some early readers heard its warnings as near-Scripture. The Catholic Church's Nostra Aetate 4 says that "the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God"; see the canon note at 4:6.

echoes: Daniel 7:7-8; Daniel 7:24; Exodus 31:18; Exodus 32:7-19; Romans 9:4-5; Romans 11:1-2; Romans 11:28-29; Matthew 22:14; Hebrews 10:25; 1 Enoch 89:61-64

settings.by: The writer, as "one of you" (4:6, 4:9)
settings.when: in what he calls "the last days" and "the lawless time" (4:9)
settings.why: To keep them from sharing the covenant with the Jews (4:6) and from going their own way alone (4:10), and to wake them before the judgment. If some readers were saying "the covenant is theirs and ours," that would explain why the writer argues so hard in the chapters that follow.
views: The Jewish Encyclopedia holds that only a live struggle between Paul's followers and Jewish Christians who "still clung to the Jewish nation in its last struggle against Rome under Bar Kokba" can account for the letter.
Ladeuze finds "no clear situation" described and calls the letter "the peaceful speculations of a catechist": on this view 4:6 frames the argument rather than reporting a party in the church.
settings.readers: Readers some of whom, the writer implies, were saying "the covenant is theirs and ours" (4:6), and some of whom kept apart from the gathering "as though you were already made right with God" (4:10).

settings.by: Daniel, as Barnabas quotes him freely
settings.to: in Daniel, readers in a time of persecution; in Barnabas, his own readers
settings.when: Daniel 7's vision of the four beasts
settings.why: In Daniel, to show that God will end the cruel kingdoms. In Barnabas, to show that the end has begun.

title: Why the Lord Suffered in the Flesh
sum: Why did the Lord, "Lord of the whole world," to whom God said "Let us make humankind," suffer at human hands (5:5)? Barnabas answers: so that we would be made clean by the forgiveness of sins (5:1); to destroy death and show the resurrection (5:6); to keep the promise to the fathers and prepare "the new people" (5:7).

He had to come "in the flesh," because no one could look at God unveiled, as no one can look into the sun (5:10). He chose sinful apostles to show he came to call sinners (5:9). And he came so that those who killed the prophets would fill up their sins (5:11). The prophets foretold the wound, the tree and the beating: Isaiah 53, Zechariah 13:7, the Psalms and Isaiah 50.

views.H: Origen, about AD 248, quotes 5:9 ("lawless beyond every kind of sin") in answering the pagan Celsus (Against Celsus 1.63), proof that the letter was known in Alexandria and Caesarea.
views.J: The chapter speaks of Israel as those who strike "their own shepherd" (5:12) and fill up their sins (5:11). Such lines are hard to read after centuries in which Christians blamed the Jewish people for Christ's death.
views.N: The chapter rests on Isaiah 53 (Acts 8:32; 1 Peter 2:24), Zechariah 13:7 (Matthew 26:31) and Isaiah 50:6-7, the passages the New Testament uses for the passion.
views.T: Everything in the chapter is read toward the cross: "Nail my flesh" (Psalm 119:120 in the Greek) becomes the nails.
views.C: The stress on Christ "in the flesh" places the letter with 1 John against those who said Christ only seemed to have a body.

echoes: Isaiah 53:5-7; Zechariah 13:7; Psalm 22:16-20; Psalm 119:120; Isaiah 50:6-7; Genesis 1:26; Matthew 9:13; 1 Timothy 3:16; 1 John 4:2

settings.by: The writer
settings.when: continuing his teaching
settings.why: To answer a question believers and outsiders asked: how could the Lord of all suffer at human hands? The answer gathers the prophets' words, so the readers see the cross as planned and foretold.

settings.by: Isaiah, about the Servant of the Lord
settings.to: in Isaiah, the exiles; in Barnabas, "us"
settings.why: In Isaiah, to show a servant suffering for others. In Barnabas, to show that the Scripture foretold Jesus' death "for us" (5:2).

title: The Stone and the Good Land
sum: Barnabas continues with the prophets. The Lord's servant, set like solid rock, is the stone of Isaiah 28:16 and Psalm 118:22; our hope is not in a stone but in his flesh set in strength (6:1-4). The Psalms foretell the gang of evildoers and the lots cast for his clothes (6:6), and Isaiah 3:10 in the Greek, the plot to bind the righteous man (6:7).

Then Moses' promise of "the good land, a land flowing with milk and honey" (6:10). Knowledge says: hope in Jesus, revealed in the flesh, because a human being is "earth that suffers" (6:9). God has made us new, a second creation (6:11-14), so that we, given life like babies first by honey and then by milk, will one day rule the earth as Genesis promised (6:17-19).

views.H: Several quotations have no known source, such as "Look, I make the last things like the first" (6:13).
views.J: The land promised to Abraham's children becomes, for Barnabas, the flesh of Jesus and the renewed believer. Philo, a Jew of Alexandria, also read the law's figures as lessons for the soul while keeping the laws themselves (see the note at 10:1); Barnabas sets the plain sense aside.
views.N: The stones of 6:2-4 are the same pair 1 Peter 2:6-7 uses. 6:12 reads Genesis 1:26 as words to the Son, as John 1:3 and Colossians 1:16 say all things were made through him.
views.T: This chapter is Barnabas's method at its boldest: land is flesh, milk and honey are the word and faith, and Genesis 1:28 is a prophecy of the age to come.
views.C: The milk-and-honey picture of new believers (6:17) is close to 1 Peter 2:2.

echoes: Isaiah 28:16; Psalm 118:22-24; Psalm 22:16-22; Isaiah 3:9-10; Exodus 33:1-3; Genesis 1:26-28; Ezekiel 36:26; Hebrews 2:5-9; 1 Peter 2:2-8

settings.by: The prophets, as quoted by the writer
settings.when: continuing from chapter 5
settings.why: To show the readers that the suffering of Christ was foretold point by point.

settings.by: Moses (6:8) and the writer's "knowledge" (6:9)
settings.to: in Exodus, Israel in the wilderness; in Barnabas, "us"
settings.when: in Exodus, after the golden calf (Exodus 33:1-3)
settings.why: In Exodus, to send Israel on to the land God promised. In Barnabas, to show that the promise speaks of Christ's flesh and of believers made new.

title: The Fast and the Two Goats
sum: The Son of God, who will judge the living and the dead, suffered so that his wound would give us life (7:2). On the cross he was given vinegar and gall (7:3), and Barnabas finds this foretold in the Day of Atonement: whoever does not fast will die; the priests alone eat the goat's entrails with vinegar while the people fast (7:3-5).

Then the two goats, "fine and alike": one goes on the altar, the other is cursed, spat on, stabbed, crowned with scarlet wool and driven into the wilderness, where its wool is laid on a thorny bush (7:6-8). The cursed goat is Christ: on that day his crucifiers will see him in a scarlet robe and say, "Isn't this the one we once crucified?" (7:9). Whoever wants the wool must reach into the thorns, as whoever wants Christ's kingdom must suffer (7:11).

views.H: Barnabas gives details Leviticus 16 lacks. The Mishnah, written down about AD 200, knows a crimson strip on the scapegoat's horns, Babylonians plucking its hair (Mishnah Yoma 6:4-8), and "the Babylonians" who ate the atonement goat raw (Mishnah Menachot 11:7). Barnabas seems to know Temple customs, or reports of them.
views.J: The Day of Atonement is Judaism's holiest day, a fast for repentance and forgiveness. Barnabas turns its rites into a picture of Jesus' death and return. The Mishnah, by contrast, preserves them as Israel's way of being cleansed (Yoma 6:8 cites Isaiah 1:18).
views.N: Hebrews 9 reads the Day of Atonement as Christ the high priest entering with his own blood. Barnabas reads the two goats instead as Christ's two comings, as Revelation 1:7 sees the pierced one coming.
views.T: The goat is "a figure of Jesus" (7:7, 7:10): likeness of the goats, scarlet wool, thorns, each detail is made to speak.
views.C: Justin Martyr also reads the two goats as "the two appearances of Christ" (Dialogue with Trypho 40), so this reading was shared among second-century Christians.

echoes: Leviticus 16:5-22; Leviticus 23:27-29; Matthew 27:28-34; Revelation 1:7; John 19:37; Hebrews 9:11-14; Genesis 22:9

settings.by: The writer, quoting commands he says "the prophet" gives (7:4) and words he gives to Christ (7:5)
settings.when: the Day of Atonement, the yearly fast
settings.why: To show that the rites of Israel's holiest day pointed to Jesus' suffering and return. In Leviticus the rite was for Israel's cleansing; in Barnabas it becomes a prophecy of the cross.

title: The Red Heifer
sum: Barnabas turns to the red heifer of Numbers 19. Sinful men offer and burn it; children gather the ashes, tie scarlet wool and hyssop to wood, and sprinkle the people (8:1). The heifer is Jesus; the sinful men are those who led him to slaughter; the sprinkling children are the apostles who preached forgiveness, twelve for the twelve tribes; the three who sprinkle stand for Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (8:2-4).

The wool on the tree means the kingdom of Jesus is "on the tree"; the hyssop that heals through its grime means believers will be saved in filthy days (8:5-6). these things are "clear to us, but dark to them" (8:7).

views.H: Numbers 19 has a priest, a heifer and a clean man; Barnabas has sinful men, children and wool on wood. The Mishnah tractate Parah tells of children raised in purity who drew the water and, in one rabbi's view, sprinkled one another (Mishnah Parah 3:2-4).
views.J: The red heifer was Israel's means of cleansing from contact with the dead,. Barnabas claims to know its hidden reason: it points to Jesus.
views.N: Hebrews 9:13-14 argues from the heifer's ashes to Christ's blood: if one cleansed the flesh, how much more will the other cleanse the conscience.
views.T: The chapter is a full allegory: each person and object in the rite stands for something in the gospel.
views.C: Hebrews 9:13-14 already reads the heifer as a figure, so Barnabas is not alone in seeing Christ there.

echoes: Numbers 19:1-22; Hebrews 9:13-14; Hebrews 9:19; Matthew 19:28; Psalm 51:7; John 19:29

settings.by: The writer
settings.when: continuing the explanation of Israel's rites
settings.why: To show that even the rite of cleansing with ashes was a figure of Jesus' death and of the apostles' preaching.

title: Circumcision of the Heart, and the 318
sum: God "circumcised our heart" and our ears, so that we hear and believe (9:1-3). The circumcision "they have trusted in" has been done away with; God never meant it in the flesh; they did it because "an evil angel" misled them (9:4). Syrians, Arabs, Egyptians and the priests of idols also circumcise, so the mark proves nothing (9:6).

Then the writer's prize: Abraham circumcised "eighteen and three hundred" men. In Greek numbers, eighteen is IH, the first letters of Jesus, and three hundred is T, the cross (9:7-8). "No one has learned a truer lesson from me" (9:9).

views.H: Lake sums up the letter's view: "The literal exegesis of the ceremonial law is to him a device of an evil angel who deceived the Jews." The number 318 comes from Genesis 14:14, joined to the circumcision of Genesis 17.
views.J: Circumcision is the sign of the covenant in Genesis 17, kept by Jews ever since as God's command. To call it the work of an evil angel is to say the Jewish people obeyed a demon; the Jewish Encyclopedia counts such claims as signs of the letter's "anti-Judaic spirit of great bitterness."
views.N: Paul argues that circumcision of the heart matters (Romans 2:28-29) and that Gentile believers should not be circumcised (Galatians 5:2-6), but he says God gave circumcision as a seal (Romans 4:11) and that it is of much value to the Jew (Romans 3:1-2).
views.T: The 318 is the letter's boldest piece of number-reading. Clement of Alexandria repeats it (Stromata 6.11).
views.C: Ladeuze reads 9:4 narrowly: what Barnabas calls the devil's work is "this purely material observance" of the rites, not the law itself.

deep.b: Greek used letters for numbers: alpha 1, beta 2, ... iota 10, and so on, with eta 8 and tau 300. Genesis 14:14 in the Greek gives Abraham's men as "eighteen and three hundred" (the Hebrew has the same order). Barnabas writes the eighteen as I and H, that is, IH, the first two letters of IĒSOUS, "Jesus," a short form later Christians used in writing the holy name. The three hundred, T, has the shape of a cross. So, he says, Abraham "received the teachings of three letters" (9:7). It works only in Greek, and only by joining Genesis 14:14, which has the number, to Genesis 17:23-27, which has the circumcision.

deep.h: An evil angel and the law
deep.b: 9:4 is the letter's hardest claim: that literal circumcision came from an evil angel's deception. Paul says the law "was arranged through angels" (Galatians 3:19), and Stephen that Israel was "given the law by the orders of angels" (Acts 7:53), but neither calls those angels evil. Second-century teachers like Marcion went further and rejected the God of the Old Testament; Barnabas never does that. For him the God of Israel is the Christian God, and the law is good, if read rightly. His quarrel is with the people who read it literally.

deep.title: Claude's theory: why the 318 mattered so much
deep.b: The writer calls the 318 the truest lesson he ever taught (9:9). A possible reason: it put the name of Jesus and the cross inside the very rite that marked Israel off, at its first institution with Abraham. If the first circumcision already pointed to Jesus, then the sign was Christian from the start, and the readers had no reason to take it up from the synagogue. This is my reading, built on 9:4-9 and 3:6; I have not seen it argued in the sources opened for this page.

echoes: Genesis 14:14; Genesis 17:9-27; Jeremiah 4:3-4; Jeremiah 9:25-26; Deuteronomy 10:16; Romans 2:28-29; Romans 3:1-2; Romans 4:9-12; Galatians 5:2-6

settings.by: The writer, quoting the Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah and Deuteronomy
settings.when: continuing his teaching
settings.why: To persuade the readers that circumcision in the flesh never mattered, and so that the Jewish people's sign of the covenant gives them no claim. If the readers were tempted to keep the Jewish law (3:6; 4:6), that would explain the force of the argument.
settings.readers: Readers who could be told that circumcision was a "seal" (9:6). Ladeuze links 9:4 to Hadrian's ban on circumcision, which on his dating puts them about AD 130.

title: What Moses Meant by the Food Laws
sum: Moses forbade the pig, birds of prey and scaleless fish, but "God's commandment is not about not eating" (10:2). Each stands for people to avoid: the pig for those who remember God only when hungry, birds of prey for those who rob instead of work, fish of the deep for the hopelessly ungodly (10:3-5).

The hare, the hyena and the weasel stand for sexual sins, by the animal lore of the time (10:6-8). David's "Happy is the person" in Psalm 1:1 knows the same three teachings (10:10). The clean animals that chew the cud and split the hoof stand for those who think over the word and walk in this world while waiting for the next (10:11). "But how could they understand or grasp these things?" (10:12).

views.H: The animal lore was common in antiquity; Clement of Alexandria repeats the hare and hyena lore and rejects it (Instructor 2.10).
views.J: Jewish writers in Alexandria also read the food laws as moral lessons while still keeping them. Philo reads chewing the cud as memory and the split hoof as telling apart the two roads of life (On the Special Laws 4.106-108). Barnabas takes the lesson and drops the law.
views.N: The New Testament frees Christians from the food laws by a different route: Jesus declares all foods clean (Mark 7:19), and Peter's vision (Acts 10) and Paul (Romans 14) follow.
views.T: This is moral allegory, close to Philo's. Barnabas adds his rule that the literal sense was never meant.
views.C: See the site's cards on the food laws at Leviticus 11 and Romans 14.

echoes: Leviticus 11:1-47; Deuteronomy 14:3-21; Psalm 1:1; Mark 7:19; Acts 10:9-16; Romans 14:14

settings.by: The writer, explaining what he says Moses meant "in the Spirit" (10:2, 10:9)
settings.when: continuing his teaching
settings.why: To show that the food laws teach whom to avoid and whom to cling to, so that the readers need not keep them as food rules.

title: The Water and the Cross
sum: Did the Lord show beforehand the water and the cross? Yes. Israel, says Barnabas, would refuse the baptism that brings forgiveness and dig "a pit of death" for themselves (11:1-3). The prophets speak of a high rock with water that does not fail (11:4-5).

Psalm 1's tree planted by the water joins the two: "Happy are those who put their hope in the cross and went down into the water" (11:8). Ezekiel's river with its life-giving trees means that "we go down into the water loaded with sins and filth, and come up bearing fruit in the heart" (11:10-11).

views.H: The chapter quotes Jeremiah 2, Isaiah 16, 33 and 45, Psalm 1 and Ezekiel 47, all in the Greek and sometimes changed: Isaiah's "mountain of Zion" becomes "my holy mountain Sinai" (11:3).
views.J: Jewish washings for purity were a living practice; Barnabas says Israel "would build something for themselves" instead of accepting baptism.
views.N: Paul ties baptism to Christ's death (Romans 6:3-4) and Peter to salvation (1 Peter 3:21). Barnabas joins tree and water in one image.
views.T: Every tree is the cross and every water baptism.
views.C: The chapter is an early witness to baptism by going down into water for the forgiveness of sins. Churches differ on what baptism does; see the site's cards at Acts 2, Acts 8 and Mark 16.

echoes: Jeremiah 2:12-13; Isaiah 33:16-18; Isaiah 45:2-3; Psalm 1:1-6; Ezekiel 47:1-12; Romans 6:3-4; 1 Peter 3:21; Revelation 22:1-2

settings.by: The writer, quoting the prophets and David
settings.when: continuing his teaching
settings.why: To show that baptism and the cross were foretold together, so that the readers value their baptism above Israel's washings.

title: The Cross, the Snake and the Name of Jesus
sum: The cross was foretold again. A prophet outside the Bible speaks of a tree bent and rising and of blood dripping from a tree (12:1). Moses, standing high with his arms outstretched while Israel fought, made "a figure of the cross" (12:2-3). Moses, who forbade images, made a bronze snake on wood, so that the bitten who hoped in it lived: a figure of the dead Christ who gives life (12:5-7).

Moses also gave Hoshea son of Nun the name Jesus (Joshua) when he sent him to spy out the land, and told him that "the Son of God" would destroy Amalek (12:8-9). And David calls the Christ "my Lord," not his son (12:10-11), as does Isaiah 45:1 in a form where "Cyrus" has become "Lord."

views.H: 12:1 is close to 4 Ezra 5:5, where blood drips from wood, as Lake's margin notes. 12:11 depends on a reading of Isaiah 45:1 that differs from the Greek by one letter (kyriō for Kyrō).
views.J: Exodus 17 ties the victory to Moses' raised hands and ends with an altar called "The LORD Is My Flag" (Exodus 17:15). Read in Jewish terms, the scene teaches that victory comes from God, not that Moses made a cross.
views.N: John 3:14 uses the bronze snake as Barnabas does. Jesus' question about David's son (Mark 12:35-37) is the source of 12:10-11, though Barnabas goes further than Jesus.
views.T: Moses' arms, the snake and Joshua's name make up the letter's fullest cluster of types for the cross and for Jesus.
views.C: Barnabas's denial that Christ is David's son (12:10) stands against the Gospels and Paul, who confess Jesus as both David's son and Lord (Romans 1:3-4).

echoes: Exodus 17:8-14; Numbers 13:16; Numbers 21:6-9; John 3:14-15; Isaiah 65:2; Psalm 110:1; Mark 12:35-37; Isaiah 45:1; 4 Ezra 5:5

settings.what: Figures of the cross and of the name
settings.by: The writer, quoting Moses, David, Isaiah and an unnamed prophet
settings.when: continuing his teaching
settings.why: To show that the cross and the name of Jesus were set down in the law and the prophets, so that the readers see the Scriptures as Christian from the start.

title: Which People Is the Heir?
sum: "Let us see whether this people is the heir, or the first one" (13:1). Barnabas answers from three stories where God chooses the younger. Rebekah hears that two peoples are in her womb and "the greater will serve the lesser" (13:2-3). Jacob crosses his hands to bless Ephraim, the younger, over Manasseh (13:4-6). And Abraham, counted righteous by faith, is made "the father of the nations who believe in God while uncircumcised" (13:7).
So, he says, "this people," the church, is first and the heir of the covenant.

views.H: Barnabas joins verses and adds words: Jacob speaks the line of Genesis 25:23, and God's promise to Abraham includes Paul's phrase about the uncircumcised.
views.J: In Genesis the younger twin, Jacob, is Israel itself (Genesis 32:28), and Esau is Edom (Genesis 36:1). Barnabas reverses the roles, making Israel the elder who must serve.
views.N: Paul uses Jacob and Esau and Abraham's faith (Romans 9:10-13; 4:9-17) to show that God's choice rests on promise. But Paul ends with "all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:26). Barnabas has no such ending.
views.T: Rebekah's twins and Joseph's sons are read as "a figure of the people to come" (13:5).
views.C: Read alone, the chapter teaches that the church replaced Israel. The Catholic Church's Nostra Aetate 4 says "the Jews should not be presented as rejected or accursed by God"; see the topic and the canon note at 4:6.

echoes: Genesis 25:21-23; Genesis 48:8-20; Genesis 15:6; Genesis 17:4-5; Romans 9:10-13; Romans 4:9-17; Galatians 4:21-31; Romans 11:26-29

settings.by: The writer, quoting Genesis
settings.when: continuing his teaching
settings.why: To answer the question raised in 4:6, whose covenant it is, by Scripture's own stories of the younger chosen.

title: The Covenant Given to Us
sum: Did God give the covenant he swore to the fathers? Yes, but Israel "were not worthy to receive it" (14:1). Barnabas retells Sinai: forty days, tablets written "by the finger of the Lord's hand," the golden calf, the tablets smashed (14:2-3). Moses received the covenant "as an attendant"; the Lord himself gave it to us, by suffering for us (14:4).

He came to ransom our hearts from darkness and set up the covenant in us (14:5-6), as Isaiah says of the Servant: a covenant for the human race, a light for the nations, sent to proclaim release and the year of the Lord's favor (14:7-9).

views.H: The quotations from Isaiah 42, 49 and 61 follow the Greek; 14:8 matches the form of Isaiah 49:6 quoted in Acts 13:47.
views.J: The chapter repeats the claim of 4:7-8 that Israel never truly received the covenant. Exodus tells that the covenant at Sinai was given, broken and renewed (Exodus 34:27-28).
views.N: Hebrews 3:5-6 contrasts Moses the attendant and Christ the Son; Luke 4:18-19 has Jesus read Isaiah 61.
views.T: The Servant songs of Isaiah are read as the Father's words to the Son.
views.C: The Servant songs became central to Christian preaching of Christ through Acts and Luke.

echoes: Exodus 24:18; Exodus 31:18; Exodus 32:7-19; Isaiah 42:6-7; Isaiah 49:6-7; Isaiah 61:1-2; Acts 13:47; Luke 4:18-19; Hebrews 3:5-6

settings.by: The writer, quoting Exodus and Isaiah
settings.when: continuing from chapter 13
settings.why: To complete the answer to 4:6: the covenant is the church's, given by the Lord himself. Read alongside Romans 9-11, it shows how far the letter goes beyond Paul.

title: The Sabbath and the Eighth Day
sum: The Ten Words command the Sabbath "with clean hands and a clean heart" (15:1). God made the world in six days and rested on the seventh; since "the Lord's day will be like a thousand years," everything will end in six thousand years (15:3-4). Then the Son will come, end the lawless one's time, judge the ungodly, change the sun, moon and stars, and "truly rest on the seventh day" (15:5).

No one can keep the day holy now, because no one is clean in heart; we will keep it when we are made holy and all things are new (15:6-7). God does not accept "the Sabbaths of the present time" but will make "the beginning of an eighth day, the beginning of another world." So "we keep the eighth day with gladness," the day Jesus rose (15:8-9).

views.H: 15:9 is an early witness to Christians keeping Sunday, called "the eighth day." The six-thousand-year scheme draws on Psalm 90:4.
views.J: The Sabbath is the sign of the covenant between God and Israel (Exodus 31:13-17), kept from Friday evening to Saturday evening. Barnabas says it cannot now be kept at all, though the law calls it a covenant "for all time" (Exodus 31:16).
views.N: Hebrews 4:1-11 speaks of a Sabbath rest still waiting for God's people. 2 Peter 3:8 gives the day-as-a-thousand-years saying.
views.T: The days of creation become the ages of the world, and the seventh day the age to come.
views.C: Christians differ on the Sabbath and Sunday: some keep Sunday as the Christian Sabbath, some keep the seventh day, some keep no Sabbath law. See the site's cards at Revelation 1, Exodus 20 and Colossians 2, and on the thousand years at Revelation 20.

echoes: Genesis 2:2-3; Exodus 20:8-11; Psalm 24:4; Psalm 90:4; 2 Peter 3:8; Isaiah 1:13; Hebrews 4:1-11; Revelation 20:4-6; Acts 20:7; Revelation 1:10

settings.by: The writer, to his "children" (15:4)
settings.when: continuing his teaching
settings.why: To show why the readers do not keep the Jewish Sabbath but keep Sunday with gladness. If they were tempted by the Jewish law (3:6), that would explain why the Sabbath gets a whole chapter.
settings.readers: Readers who already "keep the eighth day with gladness" (15:9).

title: The True Temple
sum: Israel, says Barnabas, put its hope in the building and made God holy in the temple "almost the way the nations do" (16:1-2). God himself says heaven is his throne and earth his footstool. Now "those who tore this temple down will build it themselves": the Temple was destroyed in war, and the servants of their enemies are rebuilding it (16:3-4). The Scripture foretold that the Lord would hand over the sheep, their fold and their tower (16:5).
But there is a temple of God: the believer's heart. Once full of idols, "a house of demons," it is now built anew in the name of the Lord, where God lives and speaks (16:6-10).

views.H: 16:3-4 is the second dating argument. Lake says it "is supposed to refer to the events of 132 A.D." and that neither date argument "is quite satisfactory." Cassius Dio says Hadrian built a temple to Jupiter on the site of the Temple (Roman History 69.12).
views.J: The Temple was the center of Israel's worship, and its loss in AD 70 was mourned and still is. Barnabas treats it as a mistake from the start.
views.N: Stephen's speech quotes Isaiah 66:1 against trust in the Temple (Acts 7:48-50); Paul calls believers God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16).
views.T: The building becomes a figure of the heart; the door of the temple is the mouth (16:9).
views.C: The quotation in 16:5 comes from 1 Enoch 89, which Barnabas calls "Scripture."

echoes: Isaiah 40:12; Isaiah 66:1; Isaiah 49:17; Acts 7:48-50; 1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21-22; 1 Peter 2:5; 1 Enoch 89:56; 1 Enoch 89:66

settings.by: The writer
settings.to: his readers, who once worshiped idols (16:7)
settings.when: after the destruction of the Temple in AD 70; perhaps when rebuilding was in the news (16:4)
settings.why: To turn the readers' eyes from the Temple in Jerusalem to the temple God builds in them.
views: 16:4 refers to Hadrian's building at Jerusalem about AD 130, so the letter dates from then.
16:4 refers to Jewish hopes, after AD 70, that Rome would let the Temple be rebuilt.
16:4 speaks of the new temple of 16:6-10, so it gives no date.
settings.readers: Readers whose hearts, the writer says, were once "full of idolatry" (16:7), and who knew of a rebuilding of the Temple (16:3-4), whichever date that points to.

title: The End of the First Part
sum: The writer hopes he has left out nothing that has to do with salvation. If he wrote about things present and to come, the readers would not understand, "because they lie hidden in parables" (17:1-2). So ends the letter's "knowledge" of Scripture.

views.H: The one Latin manuscript ends here, with a doxology. Lake says the general opinion is that the Latin left out the Two Ways, not that the Greek added it.
views.T: "In parables" sums up the method: the Scriptures hold riddles that only knowledge can open.
views.C: The break here is one reason the Jewish Encyclopedia thought the Two Ways "was probably attached to it by some copyist at a much later time"; Lake reports that the general opinion is the other way.

echoes: Mark 4:10-12; Hebrews 9:9; 6:10

settings.what: The close of the first part
settings.by: The writer
settings.when: before he turns to the Two Ways
settings.why: To mark that the teaching on Scripture is complete, and to hint that more lies hidden.

title: Two Ways: Light and Darkness
sum: "Now let us move on to another knowledge and teaching." There are two ways, of light and of darkness, with light-bringing angels of God over one and angels of Satan over the other. The one is Lord forever; the other rules "the present time of lawlessness" (18:1-2).
The Two Ways that follows is shared with the Didache (Didache 1-5), often word for word. Where the Greek is the same, the Plain English Translation uses the same English.

views.H: Lake's introduction to the Didache gives three possibilities: Barnabas used the Didache, the Didache used Barnabas, or both used a common source, which "probably the majority of scholars" prefer, many thinking it "a Jewish pre-Christian document, used for catechetical purposes."
views.J: The two ways go back to Deuteronomy 30:15-19 and Jeremiah 21:8. Angels over the two ways recall Jewish teaching on two spirits; the site's notes on 1 John compare the Community Rule from Qumran.
views.N: Matthew 7:13-14 has the wide and narrow roads; 1 John and Ephesians the light and darkness.
views.C: The Two Ways was used to teach new believers before baptism, as the Didache shows (Didache 7:1).

echoes: Deuteronomy 30:15-19; Jeremiah 21:8; Psalm 1:6; Matthew 7:13-14; Didache 1:1; 1 John 1:5-7; 2 Corinthians 11:14; John 12:31

settings.by: The writer, using a teaching shared with the Didache
settings.to: his readers, as moral teaching after the "knowledge" of 1-17
settings.when: the second part of the letter
settings.why: To give the readers plain commands for daily life, after the hidden meanings of chapters 1-17. Read beside the Didache, it shows a teaching that circulated among churches, which the Didache sets before baptism (Didache 7:1).
views: The Didache's Two Ways is the source.
Barnabas's Two Ways is the source.
Both used an older Two Ways, perhaps Jewish; Lake says this is probably the majority view.
settings.readers: Readers who learned the Two Ways as basic teaching. The Latin version of Barnabas lacks it (Lake), so some readers had the letter without it.

title: The Way of Light
sum: The way of light is a list of commands for those who want to reach "the appointed place" (19:1). Love the one who made you; hate hypocrisy; be humble; no sexual sin, adultery or abuse of boys (19:2-4). Do not be double-minded; love your neighbor more than yourself; no abortion or killing of newborns; teach your children to fear God (19:5).

Accept what happens as good; masters must not be bitter to slaves, and slaves must submit; share everything; guard your mouth; love your teachers like the pupil of your eye; remember the day of judgment; give without grumbling; keep what you received; make peace; confess your sins; do not pray with a bad conscience (19:6-12). "This is the way of light."

views.H: The commands match Didache 1-4 closely but in a different, looser order. Lake's footnote at 19:7 shows G copying a Didache line into Barnabas.
views.J: Much of the list echoes the Ten Commandments and Leviticus 19, as Jewish moral teaching does.
views.N: The way of light is full of New Testament teaching: love of God and neighbor, household rules (Ephesians 6), sharing (Acts 4:32), confession (James 5:16).
views.C: The ban on abortion and killing newborns (19:5) is an early Christian statement on the subject, shared with Didache 2:2.

echoes: Didache 1:2-4:14; Exodus 20:1-17; Leviticus 19:18; Deuteronomy 12:32; Ephesians 6:5-9; Acts 4:32; James 5:16; Psalm 17:8

settings.what: The commands of the way of light
settings.by: The writer, passing on a shared teaching
settings.to: his readers, each addressed as "you" in the singular
settings.when: the second part of the letter
settings.why: To set out the way to walk, so that the readers reach the appointed place. The singular "you" shows that it was meant to be heard by each person, as in a teaching for new believers.

title: The Way of the Black One
sum: The way of the Black One is crooked and full of cursing, the way of eternal death with punishment. Its sins: idol worship, brashness, the haughtiness of power, hypocrisy, a double heart, adultery, murder, robbery, pride, deceit, sorcery, greed and no fear of God (20:1).
Its people persecute the good, hate truth, ignore the widow and the orphan, lie awake for evil, kill children and destroy what God has formed, side with the rich and judge the poor lawlessly (20:2).

views.H: Barnabas's list differs from the Didache's in order and in a few items, such as "the haughtiness of power" and the widow and orphan.
views.J: The care for the widow and orphan and the hatred of idolatry come straight from the Torah and the prophets (Exodus 22:22; Isaiah 1:23).
views.N: The list is close to Paul's lists of the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:19-21; Romans 1:29-31).
views.C: "The Black One" (20:1; 4:9) is the letter's name for the devil, from its light and darkness picture.

echoes: Didache 5:1-2; Galatians 5:19-21; Romans 1:29-31; Exodus 22:22-24; Isaiah 1:17; Isaiah 1:23; James 1:27

settings.by: The writer
settings.when: after the way of light
settings.why: To show what to avoid, by listing the sins and the people of the way of death, so that the readers recognize the road.

title: Farewell
sum: It is good to learn the Lord's decrees and walk in them; whoever does will be glorified in God's kingdom, and whoever chooses otherwise will perish: "That is why there is a resurrection. That is why there is repayment" (21:1). The writer asks those who stand above others to do good, for the day is near (21:2-3).

He prays that God will give his readers wisdom, understanding and knowledge of his decrees, urges them to be taught by God and to keep every commandment while "the good vessel" of the body is with them, asks them to remember him, and says farewell to "children of love and peace" (21:4-9).

views.H: The closing title in Lake's Greek is "Letter of Barnabas," the only place the name appears.
views.N: "Taught by God" (21:6) is Paul's word in 1 Thessalonians 4:9; "the Lord is near, and his reward with him" (21:3) echoes Isaiah 40:10 and Revelation 22:12.
views.T: The letter ends where it began, with "decrees" and "knowledge" (1:2, 1:5; 21:1, 21:5).
views.C: The farewell shows a pastor more than a debater: he asks for his readers' memory and prayers and blesses them.

echoes: Isaiah 40:10; Revelation 22:12; 1 Thessalonians 4:9; 2 Corinthians 4:7; 2 Corinthians 5:10; Daniel 12:2

settings.by: The writer
settings.to: his readers, especially "those of you who stand above others" (21:2)
settings.when: at the end of the letter
settings.why: To send the readers off with a call to keep the commandments and do good before the day comes, and with his blessing.
settings.readers: Readers among whom some "stand above others" (21:2) and can do good to the rest; the writer had been with them and asks to be remembered (21:7).
